questions.question: Who made the first successful telephone call, in 1876?
questions.explanation: Bell's helper, Thomas Watson, heard the words through the wire from another room. Bell worked as a teacher of deaf people.

questions.question: Which two brothers made the first flight in a powered aeroplane, in 1903?
questions.explanation: The first flight lasted only 12 seconds and went about 37 metres. The brothers made and sold bicycles before they built planes.

questions.question: What was the name of the Stephensons' famous steam train from 1829?
questions.explanation: Rocket won a contest called the Rainhill Trials in 1829. Soon after, it pulled trains on the Liverpool and Manchester Railway.

questions.question: Which old bicycle had one huge front wheel and one tiny back wheel?
questions.explanation: It was named after two British coins, one big and one small. Riders sat very high up, so falls hurt.

questions.question: The Spinning Jenny, invented in the 1760s, was a machine for making what?
questions.explanation: Before the Jenny, a spinner made one thread at a time. With it, one worker could spin many threads at the same time.

questions.question: The mills of Lancashire in England were famous for making cloth from what?
questions.explanation: Raw cotton came by ship from places such as India and the USA. Lancashire's mills turned it into cloth to sell all over the world.

questions.question: Which inventor made the phonograph, a machine that could play back recorded sound?
questions.explanation: Edison showed the phonograph in 1877. Sound was pressed into tinfoil on a turning cylinder, and a needle played it back.

questions.question: Which man made cars cheap by using a moving assembly line?
questions.explanation: At Ford's factory the cars moved past the workers. The time to build a Model T fell from over 12 hours to about 90 minutes, so it cost much less.

questions.question: What was the machine called that sent Morse code along wires in the 1800s?
questions.explanation: Morse code turns letters into short and long signals. Telegraph wires let news cross countries in minutes.

questions.question: Which man-made waterways carried heavy goods like coal and bricks before railways?
questions.explanation: Barges could carry far more than a horse and cart on a rough road. Britain dug thousands of kilometres of canals in the 1700s and 1800s.

questions.question: In which country did the Industrial Revolution begin?
questions.explanation: Britain had plenty of coal and iron, and rivers and ports for moving goods. Its first big factories opened in the 1700s.

questions.question: Louis Braille, who was blind, invented a way of reading with what?
questions.explanation: Braille was only 15 years old when he made his dot system in 1824. Blind people read it by touching the dots with their fingers.

questions.question: How many wheels did Karl Benz's first car have?
questions.explanation: Benz's car from 1885–86 had a small petrol engine at the back. It is often called the first practical car.

questions.question: A huge hall built in London's Hyde Park in 1851 was made mostly of iron and what?
questions.explanation: So much glass was used that people called it the Crystal Palace. Its parts were made in factories and bolted together.

questions.question: What was the world's first sticky postage stamp called?
questions.explanation: It came out in Britain in 1840 and showed Queen Victoria's head. Before stamps, the person getting the letter often paid.

questions.question: In the 1800s, ships began to cross the sea without needing the wind. What powered them?
questions.explanation: The steam engine burned coal to boil water. The steam pushed pistons that turned paddle wheels or a propeller.

questions.question: The Montgolfier brothers of France became famous for building which flying machine?
questions.explanation: In 1783 their balloon carried the first people into the sky. It was made of paper and cloth and filled with hot air from a fire.

questions.question: In 1783 the Montgolfier brothers sent a sheep, a duck and a what up in a balloon?
questions.explanation: The animals were sent up first to check that the air up high was safe. They landed safely after about eight minutes.

questions.question: Early mills used a big wheel turned by flowing what?
questions.explanation: A river turned the water wheel, and gears carried the power to the machines inside the mill. This is why many mills stood beside rivers.

questions.question: What did steam locomotives burn to make steam?
questions.explanation: Coal burned in the firebox and heated water in the boiler. Many engines pulled a wagon of coal behind them, called a tender.

questions.question: Which two French brothers showed some of the first films to paying audiences in 1895?
questions.explanation: Their early films were short and silent. One showed workers leaving a factory, and another a train arriving at a station.

questions.question: Before electric light, many city streets were lit by lamps that burned what?
questions.explanation: Gas lamps were lit each evening by a lamplighter with a long pole. London got its first gas street lights in the early 1800s.

questions.question: Which city opened the world's first underground railway, in 1863?
questions.explanation: The first trains were pulled by steam engines, so the tunnels were full of smoke. Electric trains came later and made it much cleaner.

questions.question: Benjamin Franklin invented a metal rod to protect buildings from what?
questions.explanation: The rod sends the electricity from a lightning strike safely into the ground. Franklin made it in the 1750s.

questions.question: On a steam train, what was the job of the fireman?
questions.correct: To shovel coal into the fire
questions.explanation: Burning coal made the steam that moved the train. On a long trip a fireman could shovel several tonnes of coal.

questions.question: Why did 1800s factories have very tall chimneys?
questions.correct: To carry smoke up and away
questions.explanation: The tall chimney also pulled air through the fire, so it burned better. Even so, factory smoke made many towns dirty and grey.

questions.question: Miners once took canaries underground to warn them about what?
questions.explanation: Canaries are small and feel bad air quickly. If the bird became sick, the miners knew they had to leave fast.

questions.question: Early steamships had big wheels at their sides that pushed them along. What were they called?
questions.explanation: The paddles dipped into the water and turned like a mill wheel. Later ships used a propeller under the back of the ship instead.

questions.question: What does a lock on a canal do for boats?
questions.explanation: Canals cannot go straight up a hill, so locks work like water steps. Boats go into a chamber, and water is let in or out.

questions.question: The wings of the first aeroplanes were a wooden frame covered with what?
questions.explanation: Wood and cloth were light and cheap, and easy to mend. A heavier plane could not have got off the ground with the early engines.

questions.question: Which animals pulled coal carts through the low tunnels of many mines?
questions.explanation: Ponies were small enough to fit in low tunnels and strong enough to pull heavy loads. Some lived underground for most of the year.

questions.question: Which vehicles ran on rails along city streets, first pulled by horses and later powered by electricity?
questions.explanation: Trams carried many people at a low price. In many cities they let workers live further from the factories.

questions.question: Which machine with keys printed letters on paper, instead of writing by hand?
questions.explanation: Typewriters spread into offices from the 1880s. Letters could then be written neatly and much faster than by hand.

questions.question: Which machine played music from flat discs, using a needle and a big horn?
questions.explanation: Gramophones first appeared in the late 1880s. Flat discs were easier to copy than cylinders, so the same music could be sold to many people.

questions.question: Why did people have to sit very still for the earliest photographs?
questions.correct: The camera needed a long time to work
wrong: It was against the law to smile
The pictures were painted by hand
questions.explanation: Early photographs could take many seconds, or even minutes. If you moved, your face came out blurry.

questions.question: As factories grew, many people left the countryside and moved to where?
questions.explanation: Factories needed lots of workers, and towns grew very fast. Many families lived in small, crowded houses close to the factory.

questions.question: A loom is a machine used to make what?
questions.explanation: A loom weaves threads that cross over and under each other. In the 1800s, factory looms were powered by water or steam.

questions.question: What name do we give to the time when machines and factories changed how people worked, in the 1700s and 1800s?
questions.explanation: Before this time most people worked on farms or at home. Then machines made goods faster, and many people started working in factories.

questions.question: James Watt wanted to show how strong his engines were. He compared them to which animal?
questions.explanation: Watt worked out how much work a strong horse could do in a minute. This is how the unit called horsepower began.

questions.question: Which inventor sent radio signals across the Atlantic Ocean in 1901?
questions.explanation: The signal went from Cornwall in England to Newfoundland, now part of Canada. It was just the Morse letter S, three short dots.

questions.question: Which French pilot was the first to fly an aeroplane across the English Channel, in 1909?
questions.explanation: He flew from near Calais to Dover in about 36 minutes. The flight won him a prize of £1,000 from a London newspaper.

questions.question: In 1919, Alcock and Brown made the first non-stop flight across which ocean?
questions.explanation: They flew from Newfoundland to Ireland in about 16 hours, in a bomber that had been changed for the flight.

questions.question: Which woman took the first long car journey, in 1888, to show that her husband's car worked?
questions.explanation: Bertha drove about 100 kilometres without telling her husband Karl. On the way she bought fuel at a chemist's shop.

questions.question: Nikola Tesla is best known for his work on which kind of electricity?
questions.explanation: With transformers, AC can be sent far along wires at high voltage with little loss. It is the kind most homes get from the wall.

questions.question: Which English scientist found in 1831 how to make electricity with magnets and moving wire?
questions.explanation: This is called electromagnetic induction, and it is how electric generators work. Faraday's discovery lit up the modern world.

questions.question: Which Swedish chemist invented dynamite in 1867?
questions.explanation: Dynamite was safer than the liquid nitroglycerine it was made from, and was used for mines, canals and tunnels. Nobel left money for the Nobel Prizes.

questions.question: Why did Britain's railways begin to use one standard time in the 1840s?
questions.correct: So that timetables worked in every town
wrong: To save coal on the trains
To make the trains go faster
questions.explanation: Before this, each town set its clocks by the sun, so noon came at slightly different times. Trains needed the same time everywhere.

questions.question: Which railway, begun in 1891, links Moscow with Vladivostok on the Pacific coast?
questions.explanation: It is more than 9,000 kilometres long. The route through Russian land alone was finished in 1916.

questions.question: Which Frenchman announced the first practical photography process in 1839?
questions.explanation: His pictures were made on silver-coated metal plates and were called daguerreotypes. Each plate gave one single picture.

questions.question: In which country was the telephone inventor Alexander Graham Bell born?
questions.explanation: Bell was born in Edinburgh in 1847. He moved to Canada and then to the USA, where he made his telephone.

questions.question: In the late 1880s the Scottish vet John Dunlop made an air-filled tyre for his son's what?
questions.explanation: The air cushion gave a much smoother ride on rough roads. Soon bicycles and then cars used air-filled tyres.

questions.question: In the early 1800s, English workers called Luddites broke what in protest?
questions.explanation: They feared the new machines would take their jobs. The word 'Luddite' is also used for a person who dislikes new technology.

questions.question: The fast sailing ship Cutty Sark was built in 1869 mainly to carry which cargo from China?
questions.explanation: Clippers raced to bring the first tea of the year to London. Steamships and the Suez Canal soon ended the tea races.

questions.question: In the 1850s Elisha Otis made a safety brake that stops what from falling if the rope breaks?
questions.explanation: At a fair in New York in 1854, Otis stood on a raised lift while its rope was cut, and it did not fall. Safe lifts made tall buildings practical.

questions.question: Which gas filled Count Zeppelin's airships to make them float?
questions.explanation: Hydrogen is the lightest gas there is, but it burns very easily. Later airships used the safer gas helium when they could.

questions.question: Which English city was nicknamed 'Cottonopolis' because of its huge cotton mills?
questions.explanation: Raw cotton arrived at Liverpool and went by canal and rail to Manchester. The city's mills made cloth for the whole world.

questions.question: Which German region, with coal mines and steelworks, became one of Europe's biggest industrial areas in the 1800s?
questions.explanation: The Ruhr had plenty of coal, and it lay beside the River Rhine. Cities such as Essen and Duisburg grew there.

questions.question: Jethro Tull's seed drill of about 1701 helped farmers plant seeds in what way?
questions.explanation: Seeds fell into the soil at an even depth. Farmers could then hoe between the rows to keep weeds down.

questions.question: Prince Albert, husband of Queen Victoria, helped to organise which big event in London in 1851?
questions.explanation: More than six million visits were made to see machines, tools and wonders from around the world.

questions.question: Which country became famous for making safety matches, from about the 1850s?
questions.explanation: A safety match lights only when struck on the special strip on its box. The Swedish town of Jönköping became a centre of the match industry.

questions.question: Karl Drais's 1817 'running machine', moved by pushing with the feet, was an early what?
questions.explanation: It had two wheels and a steering handle but no pedals. The rider sat and pushed along the ground.

questions.question: In the early days of the telephone, calls were connected by a person using what?
questions.explanation: The operator plugged cables into sockets to link callers. Automatic exchanges came later and took over this job.

questions.question: Gustave Eiffel designed the iron frame inside which famous statue, finished in 1886?
questions.explanation: The statue was made in France and shipped to New York in pieces. Eiffel's iron frame was built to hold up its thin copper skin.

questions.question: In 1839 Charles Goodyear found that heating rubber with sulphur made it what?
wrong: Able to glow in the dark
questions.explanation: Before this, rubber went soft and sticky in heat and hard in cold. Goodyear's way made it useful for tyres and boots.

questions.question: Bakelite, made by Leo Baekeland in 1907, was the first fully man-made kind of what?
questions.explanation: Bakelite does not melt when heated and does not carry electricity. It was used for telephones, radios and plugs.

questions.question: Many workers who built the Panama Canal fell ill with diseases spread by what?
questions.explanation: Yellow fever and malaria killed many in the early years. When doctors cleared the mosquitoes, building could go on.

questions.question: What did George Eastman's 1888 Kodak camera use to make photography easy for everyone?
questions.explanation: Earlier cameras used heavy glass plates. A Kodak came loaded with film for 100 pictures, and you sent the whole camera back to be developed.

questions.question: The QWERTY keyboard layout, first used on typewriters, is named after what?
questions.correct: The first six letters in the top row
questions.explanation: Its layout was used on typewriters of the 1870s. It stayed in use on computer keyboards long after typewriters went away.

questions.question: In the 1860s Joseph Bazalgette built a huge system of what under London?
questions.explanation: Dirty water had made the River Thames smell terrible and spread illness. His sewers made the city much healthier.

questions.question: In the 1800s, workers who dug canals and railway cuttings by hand were called what?
questions.explanation: The word comes from 'navigators', the name for the canal diggers. Navvies used picks, spades and wheelbarrows.

questions.question: In which Dutch city did the Philips company begin in 1891, making light bulbs?
questions.explanation: Gerard Philips and his father Frederik started the firm. Philips later made radios, televisions and many other goods.

questions.question: In 1856 the young chemist William Perkin made a famous man-made dye by accident. What colour was it?
questions.explanation: Perkin was 18 and was trying to make quinine, a medicine for malaria. His purple dye became very fashionable in Britain and France.

questions.question: John Harrison's clocks of the 1700s helped sailors to find what at sea?
questions.explanation: His marine clocks kept good time even on a rolling ship. Comparing the clock with local time from the sun showed how far east or west the ship was.

questions.question: Josiah Wedgwood built a large English factory to mass-produce what?
questions.explanation: Wedgwood's pottery was sold across Europe. He also organised his workers carefully, which was new at the time.

questions.question: The raincoat called a 'mac' is named after the Scottish chemist who made waterproof cloth in the 1820s. Who was he?
questions.explanation: He stuck two layers of cloth together with rubber, which kept water out. Coats made this way became known as mackintoshes, or macs.

questions.question: Most electric trams of the 1890s got their power from what?
wrong: A giant battery under the seats
questions.explanation: A pole on the roof touched the wire above the street. The current went through the tram's motors and back through the rails.

questions.question: In 1869, what was used in a ceremony to finish America's first coast-to-coast railway?
questions.explanation: The last spike was tapped in at Promontory in Utah, where two railways met. The journey across the country then took days instead of months.

questions.question: Which Devon ironmonger built the first practical steam engine, in 1712, to pump water from mines?
questions.explanation: Newcomen's engine was slow and burned a lot of coal, but it worked. Watt later made it much more efficient.

questions.question: Whose water-powered cotton mill at Cromford, opened in 1771, is often called the first modern factory?
questions.explanation: Arkwright's mill ran day and night, with workers on shifts. It became the model for later factories.

questions.question: John Kay's flying shuttle of 1733 made which job much faster?
questions.explanation: Weavers could then use thread faster than spinners could make it. That gap led to new spinning machines.

questions.question: Why was Samuel Crompton's spinning machine of 1779 called the 'mule'?
questions.correct: It mixed ideas from two earlier machines
wrong: It was pulled by a mule
It was first built in a stable
questions.explanation: A mule is a cross between a horse and a donkey. Crompton's machine crossed the Jenny with the water frame.

questions.question: Which English clergyman designed the first power loom, in 1785?
questions.explanation: Power looms ran on water or steam rather than muscle. During the 1800s, weaving by hand slowly gave way to weaving in factories.

questions.question: Joseph-Marie Jacquard's loom of 1804 used punched cards to control what?
wrong: The speed of the water wheel
questions.explanation: Each hole in a card told the loom which threads to lift. Later inventors used punched cards for their own machines.

questions.question: Which Cornish engineer ran the first steam locomotive on rails, in 1804?
questions.explanation: His engine pulled iron and men along a Welsh tramway. It was too heavy for the cast-iron rails, which cracked.

questions.question: The first public railway to run steam locomotives opened in 1825 between Stockton and which other town?
questions.explanation: George Stephenson was the line's engineer, and its first engine was called Locomotion. The railway mainly carried coal.

questions.question: Which engineer built the Menai Suspension Bridge in Wales, opened in 1826?
questions.explanation: Its main span was the longest of any suspension bridge of its day. It joined the island of Anglesey to the mainland.

questions.question: Abraham Darby's 1709 breakthrough in making iron was using which fuel?
questions.explanation: Coke is made by baking coal. It was cheaper than charcoal, which came from wood, and Britain ran short of wood.

questions.question: Henry Bessemer's process of the 1850s made large amounts of which material cheaply?
questions.explanation: Air blown through melted iron burned off impurities. Steel was stronger than iron, so it was used for rails, ships and bridges.

questions.question: Humphry Davy's lamp of 1815 had a metal gauze around the flame. What was it meant to stop?
questions.correct: Setting off explosive gas in mines
questions.explanation: The gauze took heat away from the flame, so it could not light the gas outside the lamp. George Stephenson made a similar lamp in the same year.

questions.question: Which Frenchman led the building of the Suez Canal, opened in 1869?
questions.explanation: The canal let ships go from Europe to Asia without sailing round Africa. De Lesseps later tried to build a canal in Panama.

questions.question: Which giant iron steamship laid the first lasting telegraph cable across the Atlantic, in 1866?
questions.explanation: The ship was so big that she could carry the whole cable. News then crossed the ocean in minutes, not days.

questions.question: Brunel's SS Great Britain, built in 1843, was a large ship with an iron hull and what kind of drive?
questions.explanation: In 1845 she became the first large iron ship with a propeller to cross the Atlantic.

questions.question: In a diesel engine, what makes the fuel catch fire?
questions.explanation: Rudolf Diesel patented the idea in the 1890s. Diesel engines use less fuel than petrol engines for the same power.

questions.question: Nikolaus Otto's famous engine of 1876 worked in a cycle of how many strokes?
questions.explanation: The strokes are often remembered as suck, squeeze, bang and blow. Otto's engine ran on gas, but most petrol car engines use the same cycle.

questions.question: Which Frenchman built a steam-powered road vehicle in 1769, often called the first self-propelled car?
questions.explanation: It was made to pull cannons for the army. It was very heavy and moved at about walking pace.

questions.question: Which German pioneer made more than 2,000 glider flights in the 1890s, inspiring the Wright brothers?
questions.explanation: He studied the wings of birds and tested his gliders by jumping from a hill. Photos of his flights made people believe flying was possible.

questions.question: Which Danish inventor made a short powered flight on the island of Lindholm in 1906?
questions.explanation: Ellehammer's aircraft was tied to a pole, so it flew in circles. He also built a motorbike and a helicopter.

questions.question: The Danish engineer Valdemar Poulsen's 'telegraphone' of 1898 recorded sound on what?
questions.explanation: The wire was magnetised in patterns that matched the sound. The idea was used again in later tape recorders.

questions.question: Denmark's first railway, opened in 1847, ran from Copenhagen to which town?
questions.explanation: The line, about 30 kilometres long, was the start of the Danish rail network.

questions.question: In 1912 the Danish ship Selandia became the first large ocean-going ship with what kind of engine?
questions.explanation: Selandia was built in Copenhagen. Diesel engines were smaller and cleaner than steam engines and did not need stokers.

questions.question: William Fox Talbot's photography process of the 1840s let people make many prints from one what?
questions.explanation: Talbot's picture was a paper negative. Making prints from negatives stayed the basis of photography for about 150 years.

questions.question: Which inventor made the gramophone, which played flat discs instead of cylinders?
questions.explanation: Berliner's flat discs could be copied again and again. This made record companies possible.

questions.question: In 1872 Japan opened its first railway, between Tokyo and which port city?
questions.explanation: Britain helped build the line, and the first trains came from Britain. It was a sign of Japan's rapid change in these years.

questions.question: Which city opened the first electric underground railway on mainland Europe, in 1896?
questions.explanation: It was opened for Hungary's thousand-year celebrations. Its small trains ran in a shallow tunnel just below one of the city's grand avenues.

questions.question: The road surface called 'macadam' was made from layers of crushed what?
questions.explanation: John McAdam found that tight layers of small stones made hard, dry roads. Later, tar was added to make tarmac.

questions.question: Which feature helped Stephenson's Rocket of 1829 make steam quickly?
questions.explanation: The tubes carried hot gases from the fire through the water, giving a big area to heat it. Most later steam locomotives used the same kind of boiler.

questions.question: Before inventing the telegraph code, Samuel Morse worked as what?
questions.explanation: Morse was a well-known portrait painter. He began to think about the telegraph after a long trip home by sea.

questions.question: How did the Wright brothers' 1903 aeroplane tilt to one side to turn?
questions.explanation: This was called wing-warping. Wires bent the wing tips up or down, so the plane could tilt into a turn.

questions.question: Which German scientist first made and detected radio waves, in the 1880s?
questions.explanation: Hertz proved the waves were real but saw no use for them; others later used them for radio. The unit hertz is named after him.

questions.question: In 1850 Paul Julius Reuter bridged a gap in a telegraph line between Aachen and Brussels using what?
questions.explanation: The birds flew faster than a train could carry the news. Reuter later began one of the world's first news agencies.

questions.question: Which Birmingham manufacturer was James Watt's business partner?
questions.explanation: Boulton paid for the building of Watt's engines and sold them. Their firm made steam engines for mills and mines.

questions.question: Robert Owen ran a model cotton-mill village in Scotland. What was it called?
questions.explanation: Owen gave workers' children schooling and kept working hours shorter. New Lanark was named a World Heritage Site in 2001.

questions.question: In 1900 Count Zeppelin's first airship flew over which lake?
questions.explanation: The airship was built on the water, in a floating shed. Its first flight lasted about 18 minutes.

questions.question: The Crystal Palace was designed by Joseph Paxton, who worked as what?
questions.explanation: He was head gardener at a great house and had built big greenhouses. The Crystal Palace was like a giant greenhouse.

questions.question: The Pontcysyllte Aqueduct in Wales, finished in 1805, carries what high above a valley?
questions.explanation: Telford and William Jessop built it. The canal runs in an iron trough on stone pillars, more than 30 metres above the River Dee.

questions.question: The Gotthard rail tunnel, opened in 1882, cuts through the Alps in which country?
questions.explanation: It was about 15 kilometres long, the longest in the world at the time. It sped up trips between northern and southern Europe.

questions.question: In 1866 the German engineer Werner von Siemens improved the machine that turns movement into electricity. What is it called?
questions.explanation: A dynamo spins coils of wire near magnets. Siemens used electromagnets fed by the machine's own current, which made strong electricity cheap.
